title: Diversity in the Use of Electronic Mail: A Preliminary Inquiry
abstract: Interviews with professional office workers examine how electronic mail is used to manage daily work. The study finds substantial diversity in strategies and describes email as supporting information management, time management, prioritization, delegation, and task management rather than communication alone.

title: More Than Just a Communication System: Diversity in the Use of Electronic Mail
abstract: An empirical study of professional email users identifies distinct work-management strategies including prioritizing incoming messages, archiving information, and delegating work. The findings argue that email systems need flexible support for heterogeneous user practices and preferences.

title: Email overload: exploring personal information management of email
abstract: Empirical observations show that users employ email for task management and personal archiving as well as communication. Inbox contents frequently include outstanding tasks, partially read documents, and conversational threads, and important messages can be overlooked or lost during filing.

title: Attention-Sensitive Alerting
abstract: The paper presents utility-directed procedures for balancing the cost of interrupting users against the cost of delaying alerts. Its email-focused Priorities work models expected criticality and expected cost of delayed review and adapts notification decisions using message content and user context.

title: Temporal summaries of new topics
abstract: The paper defines temporal summaries for monitoring changes in news coverage as stories arrive sequentially. Sentences must be ranked before subsequent stories are observed, and the authors develop an evaluation corpus and empirically compare several temporal summarization methods.

title: Overview of the TREC 2002 Novelty Track
abstract: The TREC novelty track evaluates systems that, given an ordered set of relevant documents, identify sentences that are both relevant and novel relative to information already encountered. Thirteen groups participated in the initial evaluation.

title: Novelty Detection: The TREC Experience
abstract: This empirical analysis of the TREC novelty task studies identification of relevant new information in ordered topical document streams. It reports differences between human and system selections and finds that tracking novel opinions is harder than tracking events.

title: THU TREC 2002: Novelty Track Experiments
abstract: The paper reports Tsinghua University's experiments in the first TREC novelty track. The system investigates enrichment of short sentences, use of background knowledge, and determination of duplicated information when selecting relevant novel content.

title: Novelty and Redundancy Detection in Adaptive Filtering
abstract: The work extends adaptive information filtering by explicitly and separately modeling relevance and redundancy. Five redundancy measures are experimentally evaluated, providing transfer evidence for distinguishing useful new information from repeated material in a temporal stream.

title: ‘Show me more’: Incremental length summarisation using novelty detection
abstract: A user study compares summaries containing only novel sentences with incremental summaries that add contextual sentences. The experiments test whether novelty-only presentation is sufficient for relevance judgments or whether preserved context improves interpretation.

title: A New Approach for Multi-Document Update Summarization
abstract: The paper formulates update summarization using conditional information distance so that a summary of a later document cluster accounts for information in a prior cluster. Experiments on DUC/TAC 2007–2009 datasets compare the method with reference summaries and baseline systems.
venue: Journal of Computer Science and Technology

title: Evolutionary timeline summarization: A balanced optimization framework via iterative substitution
abstract: The paper generates correlated summaries over successive dates for evolving news topics while balancing relevance, coverage, coherence, and cross-date diversity. It evaluates generated timelines against manually created ones over multiple datasets.

title: Taking into account Inter-sentence Similarity for Update Summarization
abstract: The study augments coverage-and-length optimization for update summarization with explicit semantic sentence similarity to control redundancy. It evaluates the approach on DUC 2007 and TAC 2008 and 2009 update-summarization datasets.

title: Examining the State-of-the-Art in News Timeline Summarization
abstract: The paper systematically compares timeline-summarization strategies with full-task evaluation frameworks and introduces a larger benchmark spanning longer time periods. It provides empirical evidence about temporal coverage, date selection, and redundancy in evolving news timelines.

title: Updated Headline Generation: Creating Updated Summaries for Evolving News Stories
abstract: The task requires updating a previous headline in light of a revised article, identifying novel information while avoiding unnecessary changes. Human evaluation finds that models conditioned on the prior headline and article revisions can preserve factuality while making fewer needless edits.

title: Novelty Detection: A Perspective from Natural Language Processing
abstract: The paper surveys and empirically investigates semantic novelty detection when a target must be compared with multiple prior texts. It discusses graded novelty, redundancy, temporal information updates, and textual-entailment-based approaches to multi-source novelty judgments.

title: Systematically Exploring Redundancy Reduction in Summarizing Long Documents
abstract: The study systematically compares strategies for reducing redundancy in long-document summarization and proposes methods that balance importance with non-redundancy. Experiments on PubMed and arXiv summarization datasets measure both summary quality and redundancy.

title: Summarizing Email Conversations with Clue Words
abstract: The paper proposes an email-conversation summarization framework using quotation structure and clue words to estimate sentence importance. It empirically evaluates summarization of threaded email conversations, providing direct workplace-email evidence at the single-conversation level.

title: Single-document and multi-document summarization techniques for email threads using sentence compression
abstract: The paper compares collective multi-document summarization of an email thread with sequential per-message summarization, using Enron email and sentence compression. Experiments indicate that the collective approach performs better, while the tested compression techniques do not improve results in this genre.

title: Learning to Classify Email into “Speech Acts”
abstract: The paper develops and empirically evaluates classifiers for communicative acts in email, including categories related to requests, commitments, proposals, amendments, and refusals. This provides transfer evidence for distinguishing explicit obligations from generic message importance.

title: The nature of requests and commitments in email messages
abstract: The paper defines task-oriented requests and commitments at utterance level and validates the definitions through two manual annotation experiments on Enron email. It explicitly models requests as obligations placed on another agent and commitments as obligations accepted by an agent, including conditional cases.

title: Detecting action-items in e-mail
abstract: The paper studies automatic detection of emails that require action or response and localization of the text expressing that request. Its formulation targets sender intent and required receiver action rather than generic topical classification.

title: Classifying Action Items for Semantic Email
abstract: The Semanta system models email action items such as task assignments and meeting proposals as parts of ad-hoc workflows. A rule-based classifier is empirically evaluated, with results supporting assisted suggestions for user review rather than fully automatic classification.

title: Success of an Agent-Assisted System that Reduces Email Overload
abstract: RADAR identifies tasks contained in email, presents them in a task-centric Action List, and suggests schedules based on learned task-order models. In a large controlled email-overload evaluation, novice users assisted by both agents achieved better task performance with substantially fewer errors, while users varied in how much agent advice they followed.

title: ConvoSumm: Conversation Summarization Benchmark and Improved Abstractive Summarization with Argument Mining
abstract: The paper creates conversation-summarization datasets spanning several domains, including email threads, and benchmarks abstractive models with automatic and human evaluation. It also evaluates argument-mining structures that explicitly represent issues, viewpoints, and assertions.

title: Cascading Non-Stationary Bandits: Online Learning to Rank in the Non-Stationary Cascade Model
abstract: The paper studies online ranking when user preferences change abruptly at unknown times. It proposes non-stationary bandit algorithms, provides regret analysis, and empirically evaluates adaptation using a real-world web-search click dataset.

title: Reinforcement Online Learning to Rank with Unbiased Reward Shaping
abstract: The paper develops an online learning-to-rank method that continuously learns from user interactions while correcting position bias through inverse-propensity-based reward shaping. Empirical evaluation on standard OLTR datasets tests effectiveness and user-experience metrics under ongoing interaction.

title: Personalized Preference Drift Aware Sequential Recommender System
abstract: The paper addresses user preferences that change over time by detecting personalized drift points rather than imposing the same fixed short- and long-term pattern structure on every user. It empirically evaluates a sequential recommendation approach designed to adapt to these individual preference changes.

title: An End-to-End Personalized Preference Drift Aware Sequential Recommender System With Optimal Item Utilization
abstract: The work proposes an end-to-end sequential recommender that detects user-specific preference drift and selects interaction history relevant to the current preference state. Its experiments evaluate adaptation to dynamically changing preferences and utilization of historical items.

title: Experimenting with prequential variations for data stream learning evaluation
abstract: The paper empirically compares Basic Window, Sliding Window, and Fading Factors variants of prequential evaluation for data streams with concept drift. It tests how accurately each protocol reflects performance as distributions change over time and finds sliding-window prequential evaluation the strongest of the tested alternatives.

title: Learning Human Preferences Over Robot Behavior as Soft Planning Constraints
abstract: The paper distinguishes required behavior from merely desired behavior by representing user preferences as soft planning constraints rather than collapsing all considerations into one scalar utility. Simulated experiments examine inference of several preference types under noisy user choices, providing transfer evidence for separating mandatory requirements from defeasible preferences.

title: Lexicographically-ordered constraint satisfaction problems
abstract: The paper presents a formalism that explicitly separates hard feasibility constraints from softer preferences represented by lexicographic orderings. It analyzes algorithms for finding preferred feasible solutions and relates the approach to more general soft-constraint formalisms.

title: How Do Viewers Synthesize Conflicting Information from Data Visualizations?
abstract: Across four controlled experiments, participants sequentially view pairs of visualizations presenting cumulative, sometimes conflicting evidence. The study measures how direction, magnitude, context, and accompanying text affect synthesis of conflicting information and derives implications for presenting evolving evidence.
venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics

title: Effect of Personalized Email-Based Reminders on Participants’ Timeliness in an Online Education Program: Randomized Controlled Trial
abstract: A randomized crossover study with adult professional learners compares personalized weekly email reminders with general reminders. Personalized reminders incorporate each participant's prior progress and produced higher probability of being on time, providing empirical transfer evidence for personalized reminder content over repeated cycles.

title: Prospective memory reminders: A laboratory investigation of initiation source and age effects
abstract: Young and older adults complete prospective-memory tasks under no-reminder, self-initiated-reminder, and experimenter-initiated-reminder conditions. The experiments test whether reminders improve remembering and whether effectiveness depends on source, task type, or age.

title: Reminders supporting spontaneous remembering in prospective memory tasks
abstract: An experiment compares several reminder types for a prospective-memory task and a no-reminder condition. Different reminder formulations have different effects on later task execution, indicating that reminder usefulness depends on what aspect of the intention is cued.

title: Effects of delay and reminders on time-based prospective memory in a naturalistic task
abstract: Two experiments examine prospective-memory performance across delays of one to six days in naturalistic tasks. Performance declines over multi-day delays, while explicit reminders improve execution relative to implicit reminders, offering transfer evidence about forgetting risk, recency, and reminder value.

title: Let it go: How trusted reminders alter intention maintenance
abstract: The study crosses reminder reliability with reminder availability to test whether trusted external reminders merely duplicate internal intention maintenance or replace it. Thought probes track whether intentions remain in conscious awareness, providing empirical evidence about how reminder reliability changes ongoing maintenance of future tasks.

title: That Escalated Quickly: An ML Framework for Alert Prioritization
abstract: The paper presents a machine-learning framework for predicting alert- and incident-level actionability in security operations. Evaluation on real-world operational data measures both false-positive suppression and preservation of actionable incidents, making it useful transfer evidence for joint false-alert and omission trade-offs in high-volume workplace alerting.

title: Can Risk-Based Alerting Mitigate Cybersecurity Alert Fatigue?
abstract: The paper reformulates risk-based cybersecurity alerting as continuous prioritization and systematically evaluates alternative risk hypotheses across eight alert datasets. Its threshold-spanning evaluation directly examines the trade-off between reducing false alerts and retaining important incidents under differing review capacities.
